statistic: Arithmetic mean of three measured repeats; total range is min–max of per-repeat setup + application.
policy: Choose quantity semantics, acceptable coverage and geometry first; then compare speed within the valid method. These are conditional recommendations on synthetic data, not universal package rankings.

recommendations.preferred: Xarray with 1-D target axes for linear point interpolation; xarray-regrid conservative for meridian/parallel cells
recommendations.reason: The added xarray_axes control is fastest among the measured rectilinear linear adapters, with effectively equal smooth-field RMSE. xarray-regrid linear uses this axis-based xarray machinery with additional formatting; the original xarray adapter used 2-D point queries. All share the same physical grid and values. xarray-regrid conservative has much lower one-call time than CDO/ESMF here, but uses different cell-edge geometry and includes construction on every call. Use CDO/ESMF when their spherical cell representation is required; long fixed-grid series can amortize reusable weights. Do not interpret point-interpolation RMSE as a conservation ranking.

recommendations.preferred: Xarray 1-D target axes for full Gaussian point interpolation; choose conservative geometry explicitly
recommendations.reason: The full Gaussian source has separable axes. The xarray_axes control and xarray-regrid linear are faster here than SciPy with effectively equal smooth-field RMSE. Reduced Gaussian grids are outside this adapter. xarray-regrid conservative is fast and passes a separate meridian/parallel global integral control, but has higher smooth-field RMSE on this Gaussian fixture than CDO/ESMF conservative; centre samples are not exact cell averages, and cell geometry differs. Select by the required integral and geometry rather than one RMSE. MIR remains a candidate for supported native meteorological workflows.

recommendations.preferred: CDO bilinear for measured speed and accuracy; xESMF for a Python weight workflow
recommendations.reason: CDO and xESMF have very similar smooth-field error and complete coverage here; CDO is faster for both setup and application in this adapter. Prefer CDO conservative for cell averages requiring overlap remapping. Choose xESMF for Python integration and explicit weight management, not a measured speed advantage.

recommendations.preferred: Pyresample nearest for fast geolocated centre sampling; CDO bilinear for the tested structured swath
recommendations.reason: Pyresample nearest is the speed choice when nearest sampling and a finite search radius are acceptable. The structured-swath CDO bilinear adapter has much lower smooth-field RMSE but lower coverage. These RMSE values use different finite subsets: they do not establish an accuracy winner on a common footprint. Irregular/folded swaths need additional geometry checks; do not treat every swath as a structured cell grid.

recommendations.task: Raster CRS conversion: WGS84 → Web Mercator
recommendations.preferred: Rasterio bilinear; rioxarray for labelled-array integration
recommendations.reason: Rasterio has the best mean total time at 4096², with essentially identical RMSE and coverage across the three raster wrappers. odc-geo remains the choice among the tested adapters when retaining tiled lazy output is required; verify its chunked result separately.

recommendations.task: Raster CRS conversion: WGS84 → Swiss LV95
recommendations.preferred: Rasterio or rioxarray bilinear; no robust speed winner between them at 4096²
recommendations.reason: rioxarray has the lowest mean total at 4096², but the observed total-time ranges overlap Rasterio. Their outputs have the same measured RMSE and coverage. Prefer Rasterio for direct warp control, rioxarray for labelled arrays. odc-geo is slower here and the separate 256² chunk layout changes four finite-mask values; validate tiled LV95 output before relying on equivalence.

recommendations.preferred: Healpy native interpolation; MIR if lower smooth-field error justifies its cost
recommendations.reason: Healpy is the fastest measured native interpolation, at essentially the same RMSE as astropy-healpix and CDO bilinear. MIR has lower RMSE on this smooth field but much higher total time. Choose nearest native pixel lookup for categorical IDs; bilinear intensity interpolation does not preserve per-pixel totals.

recommendations.preferred: Pyresample nearest for categories/centre sampling; Gaussian only for justified smoothing
recommendations.reason: Nearest gives approximately the same smooth-field RMSE as CDO nearest and UXarray, with lower mean setup and application times. Gaussian reduces this smooth-field error but changes the operation into smoothing; it is not an overlap-conservative substitute. UXarray remains useful for its mesh data model, rather than a measured speed advantage in this nearest adapter.

recommendations.preferred: CDO conservative for a small number of fields; ESMPy when weights are reused many times
recommendations.reason: CDO and ESMPy have nearly identical smooth-field RMSE and complete coverage. CDO constructs weights faster; ESMPy applies them faster. Using mean setup + N × mean application gives an illustrative crossover near 257 fields on this fixture. This assumes the same geometry/masks and reusable weights; verify integral conservation independently. TempestRemap/NCO large regional overlap pilots timed out, so this suite supplies no completed large speed ranking for them.

recommendations.preferred: Xugrid when planar mesh geometry is appropriate; no measured cross-tool winner
recommendations.reason: Xugrid is the only adapter in this separate mesh-centred family. Its small smooth-field RMSE and fast application support suitability for this fixture, not superiority over raster or spherical adapters with different targets. Reuse weights to amortize setup; never apply planar lon/lat overlap as though it were spherical.

Use pyproj when the requested output is transformed coordinates. It performs a different task from raster reprojection; the table reports maximum round-trip coordinate error instead of field RMSE. Do not rank its speed against raster interpolation.

interpretation: Choose quantity semantics, acceptable coverage and geometry first; then compare speed within the valid method. These are conditional recommendations on synthetic data, not universal package rankings.
Arithmetic mean of three measured repeats; total range is min–max of per-repeat setup + application.

Setup and application are separate. Fused APIs include weight/geometry work in application; CDO includes native file I/O and process launch. These are measured workflows, not isolated kernel timings. The local mesh family has different targets and cannot be ranked against raster targets.

RMSE is against a smooth analytic scalar field on each output’s finite cells; it does not measure conservation, categorical correctness, edge preservation or uncertainty. Different coverage can hide difficult cells. Validate error on a common footprint and test real fields before adopting a recommendation.

For repeated fields on fixed grids, estimate setup + N × application rather than multiplying total time by N. Reuse weights only when coordinates, bounds, masks, method and periodicity match. The crossover estimate is illustrative, not a new measured multi-field benchmark.

Chunked choice: use xarray linear for separable rectilinear data, xESMF for curvilinear reusable weights, and odc-geo for the tested tiled lazy CRS workflow. All use the common 4 × 512 × 512 cube. xESMF compute changes from 5.36 s to 0.084 s between (1,128,128) and full-cube chunks, but uses full-horizontal output chunks in both; this is not evidence of distributed spatial output. odc-geo LV95 has four mask differences at (1,256,256). The NetCDF control is warm-cache only. See the chunked results for graph timings and full accuracy checks.

Non-float preferences follow semantics below: nearest for nominal classes, explicit mode for an area-majority class, conservative density/area conversion for counts, and explicit logical rules for flags. The smooth-field RMSE ranking supplies no evidence that bilinear is suitable for these variables.

External benchmark comparison: CNES reverses our historical SciPy/2-D-query xarray ordering; the new 1-D-target control now shows xarray faster locally too; xarray-regrid changes order with chunk layout; cloud tile readers can change Rasterio/rioxarray/odc-geo performance. Consult the External benchmarks page. pyinterp and MBTempest remain untested local candidates, not measured local winners.

xarray-regrid is now measured locally. The new xarray_axes control uses the same canonical destination via 1-D axes, while the historical xarray adapter uses 2-D point queries. All physical grid sizes and hashes remain shared. Conservative xarray-regrid cell edges follow meridians/parallels; ESMF edges are great circles. Its public accessor combines construction and application, so no separate reusable-weight speedup is claimed.
